drink:Bandol rouge.name: Bandol rouge
drink:Bandol rouge.teaser: Mourvèdre by law, eighteen months in wood by law: the one Var red made to wait a decade
drink:Bandol rouge.story: Bandol's rules make the red slow on purpose. At least half the blend must be Mourvèdre, and the wine spends a minimum of eighteen months in wood, mostly big old foudres, before it can be sold. Mourvèdre ripens late and only finishes properly on warm, sea-facing ground, which is what the Bandol terraces give it: a limestone and marl amphitheatre climbing from the coast, up to about 300 metres at Pibarnon. Opened young, it is tannic and closed, smelling of leather, black olive and garrigue more than fruit. Given ten years or more in bottle, the tannin softens and the fruit and spice come forward.
drink:Bandol rouge.why: Order a bottle at least eight to ten years old if the list has one, and ask for it decanted.
facts: Dark and firm; leather, black olive, garrigue herbs and liquorice, with fruit arriving only after years in bottle
Bandol AOC, red; the vintage matters, since young bottles are hard going
Un Bandol rouge, carafé. Names: Domaine Tempier (Le Plan-du-Castellet), Château de Pibarnon (La Cadière-d'Azur), Château Pradeaux (Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer), Domaine du Gros'Noré (Le Castellet)

drink:Bandol rosé.name: Bandol rosé
drink:Bandol rosé.teaser: Deeper in colour and built on Mourvèdre, this is the rosé you pour with fish soup, not by the pool
drink:Bandol rosé.story: Bandol rosé shares the red's grape. Tempier's runs at roughly 55 percent Mourvèdre, which gives it more colour, grip and length than the pale pinks sold all along the coast. The American importer Kermit Lynch began shipping Tempier from the late 1970s, and for many wine drinkers abroad that bottle was the first proof that a Provençal rosé could be serious. It holds up to bouillabaisse, aïoli and even grilled lamb, and unlike most rosé it gains from a year in the cellar. The pale fashion bottles have their own warning card in the guide.
drink:Bandol rosé.why: Drink it with the grand aïoli or a fish soup, and do not be afraid of last year's vintage.
facts: Salmon to copper rather than onion-skin pale; peach, orange peel, dried herbs and a firm, saline finish
Bandol AOC, rosé; a vintage a year or two old is often better than the newest
Un Bandol rosé. Names: Domaine Tempier, Château de Pibarnon, Domaine de la Bégude

drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.name: Côtes de Provence rosé
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.teaser: Pressed pale, dry and drunk young: the bottle on almost every table between Toulon and Saint-Tropez
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.story: Côtes de Provence is the largest appellation in Provence, about 20,000 hectares, and close to nine bottles in ten it makes are rosé. The grapes are mostly Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah, with some Rolle, picked early and pressed quickly so the juice barely takes colour. The result should be bone-dry, cool and light. Quality runs from industrial to properly fine, and the price is no guide. It is made to be drunk in the year after the harvest: older bottles fade fast. For more depth at a lower price, look inland to Coteaux Varois en Provence around Brignoles.
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.why: Ask for the most recent vintage, served very cold, and leave last year's bottle on the shelf.
facts: Pale pink; red currant, citrus peel, white pepper; dry, light, quick finish
Côtes de Provence AOC and the latest vintage; sub-zones such as Sainte-Victoire or La Londe on some bottles
Un rosé de l'année, bien frais. Names: Château Minuty (Gassin), Domaines Ott, Clos Mireille (La Londe-les-Maures), Château Léoube (Bormes-les-Mimosas), Château de Berne (Lorgues)

drink:Pastis.name: Pastis
drink:Pastis.teaser: Anise, liquorice and herbs turned cloudy with cold water: the coast's evening ritual, made just next door
drink:Pastis.story: Pastis is not a Var drink, though the Var drinks plenty of it. Paul Ricard launched his in Marseille in 1932, one of many anise drinks that filled the gap after France banned absinthe in 1915. The method matters: about one part pastis to five of cold water, poured in that order, then ice, so the anethole turns the glass milky without clumping. Most bars pour Ricard or Pastis 51. For a glass where the herbs come through past the liquorice, ask for Henri Bardouin from Forcalquier, made with more than sixty plants and spices.
drink:Pastis.why: Ask for a Bardouin at the café bar and add the water yourself from the carafe.
facts: Clear amber turning cloudy yellow with water; star anise, liquorice, fennel, garrigue herbs
Pastis de Marseille on the classic brands; Bardouin names its herbs on the back
Un pastis, or un Bardouin. Names: Ricard and Pastis 51 (Marseille), Henri Bardouin, Distilleries et Domaines de Provence (Forcalquier)

drink:Fleur de Figue.name: Fleur de Figue
drink:Fleur de Figue.teaser: A fig liqueur from Taradeau, drunk neat after dinner or splashed into cold rosé before it
drink:Fleur de Figue.story: Figs are a Var obsession, and the Solliès growers and their violet fig have their own cards in this guide. This liqueur, macerated and bottled in the Var at Taradeau, puts the fruit in a small glass: late summer, honeyed and dark. The Liquoristerie de Provence, the maker named for it, works by macerating and infusing real plants and fruit rather than adding synthetic flavour, and holds the state's Entreprise du Patrimoine Vivant label. Drink it as a digestif, or add a spoonful to cold rosé or sparkling wine for an apéritif.
drink:Fleur de Figue.why: Try it as a kir: a spoonful in a glass of chilled rosé before dinner.
facts: Deep amber; ripe fig, honey and a little spice, sweet but not syrupy

Une liqueur de figue en digestif, or un kir à la figue. Names: Liquoristerie de Provence, Château de Saint-Martin estate, Taradeau; check the current range, as we could not find this bottle listed online in Oct 2026

drink:Chestnut liqueur.name: Chestnut liqueur
drink:Chestnut liqueur.teaser: Collobrières turns its chestnuts into everything, and in October that includes the after-dinner glass
drink:Chestnut liqueur.story: In the Maures, chestnut groves cover the slopes around Collobrières, and the village calls itself the chestnut capital of the coast. The Confiserie Azuréenne, whose story is told on its own card in the tables, turns the harvest into crème de marrons, marrons glacés and a chestnut liqueur. The liqueur is sweet, nutty and a little smoky, an autumn drink rather than a summer one. The timing is right now: the village chestnut fêtes fill three Sundays in October, and in 2026 the last two fall on 18 and 25 October.
drink:Chestnut liqueur.why: Buy a bottle at the confiserie in Collobrières on a fête Sunday, alongside a tin of crème de marrons.
facts: Liqueur de châtaigne, made in Collobrières
Une liqueur de châtaigne, neat or over ice, or a spoonful of crème de marrons over vanilla ice cream. Names: Confiserie Azuréenne (Collobrières)

bars:Superbuvette.name: Superbuvette
bars:Superbuvette.teaser: A Montréal-trained wine hand pours only living wine in central Toulon, with vinegar-pickled eggs
bars:Superbuvette.story: Sarah Pinelle distributed natural wine in Montréal before opening this small cave-bar in central Toulon. The room is furnished with second-hand pieces, there is a terrace, and everything poured is natural or 'living' wine, from an Ardèche red by the glass to skin-contact bottles from Alsace. The food is a short plate of snacks: seasonal vegetable dips, hard-boiled eggs marinated in vinegar, pélardon goat's cheese from the Gard and Var olives. Le Fooding and Raisin both list it. Nobody here talks down to you about wine.
bars:Superbuvette.why: Ask what she has open by the glass and let her choose the next one.
facts: Natural wine only, by the glass or bottle; snacks
An Ardèche red by the glass from about EUR 5, skin-contact bottles around EUR 35 (Le Fooding, seen Oct 2026); listed 17:00–23:00, days not confirmed, so check

bars:Les Quilles.name: Les Quilles
bars:Les Quilles.teaser: One of Toulon's first natural-wine shops: a tiny room on the place d'Armes where the owner chooses for you
bars:Les Quilles.story: Stéphane Andréani left a job in transport and opened Les Quilles in 2010 on the place d'Armes. The shop measures about 30 square metres, and the reason to come is the man behind the counter. His list leans natural and gives plenty of room to Var growers working Carignan and Grenache, along with Bandol reds and bottles from further afield, such as Gramenon, Fanny Sabre and Domaine Labet. Gault&Millau calls it one of the town's first organic wine shops and still a reference, and there is a whisky shelf too. You can drink a glass on site.
bars:Les Quilles.why: Tell him what you are eating tonight and leave with his three suggestions.
facts: Natural and organic wine, Var and Bandol bottles to the fore; a glass on site; whisky

bars:La Dégust' Nature.name: La Dégust' Nature
bars:La Dégust' Nature.teaser: Over 300 natural wines to drink at the counter or take away, with tapenade and a cheese board
bars:La Dégust' Nature.story: La Dégust' Nature is a wine bar and shop with more than 300 natural wines on its list, to open on the spot or carry home. The owner knows the natural-wine growers well and will talk you through them. Plates are simple: charcuterie and cheese boards, house spreads such as a sea tapenade and an oriental-spiced dip, and vegetarian options, with spirits behind the bar. Listings point to local, seasonal and often organic produce. Raisin places it on boulevard de Bazeilles, not on the market street the old guide gave, so check the address before you set out.

bars:Bar du Sube.name: Bar du Sube
bars:Bar du Sube.teaser: The first-floor balcony of an old quayside hotel, looking straight down on the yachts of Saint-Tropez
bars:Bar du Sube.story: The Sube is a modest hotel on the quai de Suffren, and its bar is up one floor, with a balcony said to be the oldest in Saint-Tropez. From the few tables at the rail you look straight down on the harbour: tenders nosing in, crews hosing decks, sailing yachts warping off the quay. Inside, the bar is dark mahogany with model boats, a fireplace and Art Deco panelling, more yacht club than nightclub, with a nod to the town's Voiles regatta. Tapas are served at lunch and dinner. The drink costs what drinks cost on this quay, and the view comes free.
bars:Bar du Sube.why: Get to the balcony early and take a table at the rail; there are only a handful.
facts: Hôtel Le Sube, 23 quai de Suffren, first floor, on the Saint-Tropez port
Cocktails, rosé, tapas at lunch and dinner

bars:The Belrose terrace.name: Villa Belrose terrace
bars:The Belrose terrace.teaser: A hillside terrace in Gassin where the whole gulf spreads out below a glass of rosé
bars:The Belrose terrace.story: The Villa Belrose, an Althoff hotel and a member of the Leading Hotels of the World, sits on a Gassin hillside a few minutes from Saint-Tropez but far from its traffic. The terrace hangs above the pool and the gulf, and the yachts at anchor look like toys. People come up for one thing: a cold glass of Provence rosé while the evening light runs long over the water and the town lights come on across the bay. It is the quietest of the hotel terraces above Saint-Tropez, and the drink, not dinner, is the reason to climb.
bars:The Belrose terrace.why: Come up for the apéritif in the last hour of daylight and sit on the gulf side of the terrace.
facts: Hôtel Villa Belrose, on the Gassin hillside above the gulf

bars:Le Soleil d'Eau, La Messardière.name: Le Soleil d'Eau, La Messardière
bars:Le Soleil d'Eau, La Messardière.teaser: Turrets, domes and umbrella pines: an apéritif at a 19th-century folly above Saint-Tropez
bars:Le Soleil d'Eau, La Messardière.story: La Messardière was built in the 19th century as a wedding present: the cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d'Angeac gave it to his daughter Louise and her husband, the cavalry officer Henry Brisson de La Messardière. It is all turrets, domes and arcades, set in about ten hectares of umbrella pines and cypress on the hill above town. Airelles took it over in 2019 and reopened it as a palace hotel in July 2021. The drink is on the terrace of its bar, Le Soleil d'Eau, with the gulf below and the smell of hot pine resin in the air.
bars:Le Soleil d'Eau, La Messardière.why: Take the apéritif on the terrace as the gulf turns gold, then look back at the château lit up.

bars:La Réserve à la Plage.name: La Réserve à la Plage
bars:La Réserve à la Plage.teaser: Philippe Starck's pared-back cabana on Pampelonne: lunch on the sand without the DJ
bars:La Réserve à la Plage.story: Michel Reybier opened La Réserve à la Plage in 2019 as the beach arm of his five-star hotel, La Réserve Ramatuelle. Philippe Starck designed it to look understated: pale wood, linen, bohemian rather than bling. The menu is Mediterranean and made for sharing, overseen from the kitchen of La Voile, the hotel's starred restaurant, which has its own card in the tables. MICHELIN lists it. It is calm and design-led, a serious restaurant that happens to stand on the sand, and you pay for that calm. Nobody dances on the tables here.
bars:La Réserve à la Plage.why: Book lunch, then take a sunbed for the afternoon instead of rushing off.

bars:Moorea and Loulou.name: Moorea and Loulou
bars:Moorea and Loulou.teaser: A beach dating from 1952 and a 2019 newcomer on the same stretch: the two ages of Pampelonne
bars:Moorea and Loulou.story: Moorea is old Pampelonne. It traces itself to 1952, when it began as a bamboo straw hut with a barbecue and a few mattresses, and it still serves lunch only, raw fish and plates to share. Loulou arrived in 2019, run by the Loulou Group, with 1950s Riviera styling and a name that pays homage to Loulou de la Falaise, Yves Saint Laurent's muse. Loulou is firmly in the see-and-be-seen tier, with a designer crowd and high minimums on sunbeds and tables. Moorea's straw-hut beginnings no longer show in its prices either.
bars:Moorea and Loulou.why: For the old Pampelonne feel, pick Moorea at lunch; for the scene, book Loulou.
facts: Pampelonne, Ramatuelle: Moorea on chemin des Moulins; Loulou on the Pampelonne beach

bars:Nikki Beach.name: Nikki Beach
bars:Nikki Beach.teaser: DJ, pool, magnums and dancing on the daybeds: the Pampelonne club much of the beach now copies
bars:Nikki Beach.story: Nikki Beach came from Miami Beach and opened on Pampelonne in summer 2002, the brand's first outpost outside Miami, with an opening party people on the strip still mention. It set the formula of DJ, pool, magnums and dancing on the daybeds that much of Pampelonne now follows. The site was fully renovated in 2024. The old guide reports that from July 2026 its restaurant runs under a new name, Maurice à la Plage, while the club stays Nikki Beach. It is loud, expensive and built to please a crowd, with daybed minimums and a bill that climbs once the music does.
bars:Nikki Beach.why: Come for the long lunch on a weekend in high summer, when the DJ is on; otherwise go elsewhere.

bars:Les Caves du Roy.name: Les Caves du Roy
bars:Les Caves du Roy.teaser: The Byblos basement that has run Saint-Tropez nights since July 1967, behind a famously hard door
bars:Les Caves du Roy.story: The Byblos opened on 27 May 1967, a mock Provençal hamlet in apricot and salmon stucco built by the Lebanese businessman Jean-Prosper Gay-Para, inspired, the story goes, by Brigitte Bardot. Bardot and Mireille Darc were its godmothers. Its cellar club, Les Caves du Roy, opened that July with Juliette Gréco, Françoise Sagan and Jacques Chazot at the launch. Within months Gay-Para sold to Sylvain Floirat, on 19 September 1967, after the Six-Day War called him back to Beirut, and the Floirat family has kept the hotel since. The door is very selective, and there is no cover charge as such, only an unspoken table minimum and champagne by the magnum.
bars:Les Caves du Roy.why: Go on a weeknight in July or August, dress up, and arrive after midnight.
facts: Hôtel Byblos, 20 avenue Paul Signac, Saint-Tropez
Champagne by the magnum, cocktails; table service
